putnam-2017-a1.title: A candidate set and a chain of deductions
putnam-2017-a1.body:
**Claim:** $S = T_0 := \{n\ge2 : 5\nmid n\}$, so the integers not in $S$ are $1$ and the multiples of $5$.

**$T_0$ satisfies (a)–(c)**, hence $S\subseteq T_0$. (a) $2\in T_0$. (b) If $n^2\in T_0$ then $n^2\ge2$, so $n\ge2$, and $5\nmid n^2$ gives $5\nmid n$. (c) If $n\in T_0$ then $5\nmid n+5$, so $5\nmid(n+5)^2$, and $(n+5)^2\ge2$.

**Every set $T$ satisfying (a)–(c) contains $T_0$.** First, (c) then (b) give:

(d) if $n\in T$ then $n+5\in T$, hence $n + 5k\in T$ for all $k\ge0$.

Now:
- $2\in T$ ⇒ (c) $7^2 = 49\in T$ ⇒ (c) $54^2\in T$ ⇒ (d) $56^2 = 54^2 + 5\cdot44\in T$ ⇒ (b) $56\in T$.
- $56$ ⇒ (d) $121 = 56+65\in T$ ⇒ (b) $11\in T$ ⇒ (d) $16\in T$ ⇒ (b) $4\in T$ ⇒ (d) $9\in T$ ⇒ (b) $3\in T$.
- $16$ ⇒ (d) $36\in T$ ⇒ (b) $6\in T$.

So $2,3,4,6\in T$, and by (d) $T$ contains every $n\ge2$ congruent to $2,3,4$ or $1\pmod 5$ — that is, all of $T_0$. In particular $T_0\subseteq S$, so $S = T_0$.

**Answer:** the positive integers not in $S$ are $1$ and all multiples of $5$.

putnam-2017-a2.title: A linear recursion with the same quadratic invariant
putnam-2017-a2.body:
Define integer polynomials $P_0 = 1$, $P_1 = x$, $P_n = xP_{n-1} - P_{n-2}$ ($n\ge2$). Clearly $P_n\in\mathbb Z[x]$, and $\deg P_n = n$ (leading coefficient $1$), so $P_n\neq0$.

**Invariant.** Let $D_n = P_{n-1}^2 - P_nP_{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$. Then $D_2 = x^2 - (x^2-1)\cdot1 = 1$, and
$$D_{n+1}-D_n = P_n^2 - P_{n+1}P_{n-1} - P_{n-1}^2 + P_nP_{n-2} = P_n(P_n+P_{n-2}) - P_{n-1}(P_{n+1}+P_{n-1}) = P_n\cdot xP_{n-1} - P_{n-1}\cdot xP_n = 0.$$
So $P_{n-1}^2 - P_nP_{n-2} = 1$ for all $n\ge2$.

**$Q_n = P_n$.** By induction: $Q_0 = P_0$, $Q_1 = P_1$; if $Q_{n-1} = P_{n-1}$ and $Q_{n-2} = P_{n-2}$ (a nonzero polynomial), then as rational functions
$$Q_n = \frac{P_{n-1}^2-1}{P_{n-2}} = \frac{P_nP_{n-2}}{P_{n-2}} = P_n .$$
Hence each $Q_n$ equals the integer polynomial $P_n$. ∎

putnam-2017-a2.title: Chebyshev polynomials
putnam-2017-a2.body:
With $P_n$ as in the first solution, we show $P_{n-1}^2 - P_nP_{n-2} = 1$ in another way; the rest of the argument is the same.

For $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ we claim $P_n(2\cos\theta) = \frac{\sin((n+1)\theta)}{\sin\theta}$. This holds for $n = 0,1$ ($\sin2\theta = 2\cos\theta\sin\theta$), and the right side satisfies the same recursion because $\sin((n+1)\theta) + \sin((n-1)\theta) = 2\cos\theta\,\sin(n\theta)$.

Using $\sin(u+v)\sin(u-v) = \sin^2u - \sin^2v$ with $u = n\theta$, $v = \theta$:
$$P_{n-1}^2 - P_nP_{n-2}\Big|_{x=2\cos\theta} = \frac{\sin^2(n\theta) - \sin((n+1)\theta)\sin((n-1)\theta)}{\sin^2\theta} = \frac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = 1 .$$
So the polynomial $P_{n-1}^2 - P_nP_{n-2} - 1$ vanishes on the infinite set $(-2,2)$, hence is identically zero. ∎

putnam-2017-a3.title: Subtract a zero integral
putnam-2017-a3.body:
Put $I_0 = \int_a^bf$ as well. For $n\ge0$, using $\int_a^b(f-g) = 0$,
$$I_{n+1}-I_n = \int_a^b\left(\frac fg\right)^{n+1}(f-g)\,dx = \int_a^b\left(\left(\frac fg\right)^{n+1}-1\right)(f-g)\,dx .$$
At each point the two factors have the same sign ($f>g\iff f/g>1$), so the integrand is continuous and $\ge0$, and it is $>0$ wherever $f\ne g$. Since $f\ne g$ at some point, and hence on a small interval by continuity, the integral is positive: $I_{n+1}>I_n$.

**Divergence.** If $f\le g$ everywhere, then $\int(g-f) = 0$ with $g - f\ge0$ continuous would force $f = g$. So $f(t)>g(t)$ for some $t$, and by continuity there are $c>1$ and an interval $J\subseteq[a,b]$ of positive length with $f\ge cg$ on $J$. Then
$$I_n\ge\int_J f\left(\frac fg\right)^n dx\ge c^n\int_J f\,dx,$$
and $\int_Jf>0$ because $f>0$. Hence $I_n\to\infty$. ∎

putnam-2017-a3.title: Log-convexity via Cauchy–Schwarz
putnam-2017-a3.body:
Let $I_0 = \int_a^b f>0$. For $n\ge0$, Cauchy–Schwarz applied to $\sqrt{f^{n+1}/g^n}$ and $\sqrt{f^{n+3}/g^{n+2}}$ gives
$$I_{n+1}^2 = \left(\int_a^b\frac{f^{n+2}}{g^{n+1}}\right)^2\le\int_a^b\frac{f^{n+1}}{g^n}\int_a^b\frac{f^{n+3}}{g^{n+2}} = I_nI_{n+2},$$
so the ratios $I_{n+1}/I_n$ are nondecreasing in $n$. Also
$$I_1 - I_0 = \int_a^b\frac{f}{g}(f-g) = \int_a^b\frac{f}{g}(f-g) - \int_a^b(f-g) = \int_a^b\frac{(f-g)^2}{g}>0,$$
since the integrand is continuous, $\ge0$ and not identically $0$. Hence $r = I_1/I_0>1$, and $I_{n+1}/I_n\ge r>1$ for all $n\ge 0$. Thus $I_{n+1}>I_n$ and $I_n\ge r^nI_0\to\infty$. ∎

putnam-2017-a4.title: Sliding window over sorted scores
putnam-2017-a4.body:
Let $T = 7.4N$. The total score $14.8N$ is an integer, so $5\mid N$ and $T$ is an integer. It suffices to find $N$ students with total score $T$ (the others then also total $T$).

Sort the scores $a_1\le a_2\le\dots\le a_{2N}$ and let $s_i = a_{i+1}+\dots+a_{i+N}$ for $i = 0,\dots,N$. Then $s_{i+1}-s_i = a_{i+N+1}-a_{i+1}\ge0$ and $s_0+s_N = 2T$, so $s_0\le T\le s_N$. If some $s_i = T$ we are done. Otherwise let $i$ be the largest index with $s_i<T$; then $i<N$ and $s_{i+1}>T$.

Consider the $N+1$ students with scores $a_{i+1},\dots,a_{i+N+1}$, whose total is $s_i + a_{i+N+1}$. Dropping one student of score $v$ leaves total $T$ exactly when
$$v = s_i + a_{i+N+1} - T .$$
This $v$ is an integer with $v - a_{i+1} = s_{i+1}-T>0$ and $a_{i+N+1}-v = T - s_i>0$, so $a_{i+1}<v<a_{i+N+1}$. Since every score from $0$ to $10$ occurs, some student has score $v$, and because the list is sorted, that student's index lies strictly between $i+1$ and $i+N+1$. Dropping that student from the $N+1$ gives $N$ students with total $T$, i.e. average $7.4$. ∎

putnam-2017-a4.title: Swap students to shrink the gap
putnam-2017-a4.body:
As above $T = 7.4N$ is an integer and the total $2T$ is even. Split the class arbitrarily into groups $A$, $B$ of $N$ students; let $\Sigma A,\Sigma B$ be their totals. Then $\Sigma A - \Sigma B = 2T - 2\Sigma B$ is even.

Suppose $\Sigma A>\Sigma B$, so $\Sigma A-\Sigma B\ge2$. **Claim:** some student in $B$ has a score $v$ and some student in $A$ has score $v+1$. If not, let $v_0$ be the smallest score in $B$. Score $v_0+1$ (if $\le10$) occurs but not in $A$, so it occurs in $B$; then $v_0+2$ is not in $A$, so it is in $B$, and so on. Hence $A$ contains no score above $v_0$, so $\Sigma A\le Nv_0\le\Sigma B$, a contradiction.

Swapping these two students changes the difference to $\Sigma A-\Sigma B-2\ge0$. Repeating, after finitely many swaps the totals are equal, i.e. both groups average $7.4$. ∎

putnam-2017-a5.title: Generating function at a cube root of unity
putnam-2017-a5.body:
**Length of the game.** Let $p_n(m)$ be the probability that the game with $n$ cards lasts exactly $m$ turns, and $P_n(X) = \sum_mp_n(m)X^m$, with $P_0 = 1$. The first draw is card $k$ with probability $\frac1n$; if $k = 1$ the game ends, otherwise it continues exactly like a game with the $k-1$ cards $1,\dots,k-1$. Hence
$$P_n(X) = \frac Xn\sum_{k=1}^nP_{k-1}(X).$$
Comparing $nP_n = X\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}P_k$ with $(n-1)P_{n-1} = X\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}P_k$ gives $nP_n = (X+n-1)P_{n-1}$, so
$$P_n(X) = \frac{X(X+1)(X+2)\cdots(X+n-1)}{n!}.$$

**Who leads.** $A$ wins iff the number of turns is $\equiv1\pmod 3$, $B$ iff $\equiv2$, $C$ iff $\equiv0$. Let $a_n,b_n,c_n$ be the winning probabilities ($a_n+b_n+c_n=1$) and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$. Then
$$z_n := P_n(\omega) = c_n + a_n\omega + b_n\omega^2 .$$
Using $1+\omega+\omega^2 = 0$ one computes $\operatorname{Re}(z_n\overline\omega) = a_n - \frac{b_n+c_n}2 = \frac{3a_n-1}{2}$, and similarly $\operatorname{Re}(z_n\overline{\omega}^2) = \frac{3b_n-1}2$, $\operatorname{Re}(z_n) = \frac{3c_n-1}2$. Writing $z_n = |z_n|e^{i\varphi_n}$ ($z_n\ne0$ since no factor $\omega + j$ vanishes), $\operatorname{Re}(z_n\overline{\omega}^k) = |z_n|\cos(\varphi_n - \tfrac{2\pi k}{3})$. Hence the player with direction $\omega^k$ ($A$: $k=1$, $B$: $k=2$, $C$: $k=0$) has *strictly* the highest probability whenever $\varphi_n$ is within less than $\frac\pi3$ of $\frac{2\pi k}{3}$ modulo $2\pi$: that direction is then strictly the closest of the three, so its cosine is strictly the largest.

**The argument.** $\arg\omega = \frac{2\pi}3$, and for $j\ge1$, $\omega+j = (j-\frac12)+\frac{\sqrt3}2i$ has argument $\theta_j = \arctan\frac{\sqrt3}{2j-1}\in(0,\frac\pi3]$. So we may take
$$\varphi_n = \frac{2\pi}3 + \sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\theta_j .$$
Since $\theta_j\ge\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2j-1}$ (as $\arctan y\ge y/2$ for $0\le y\le\sqrt3$), $\sum\theta_j = \infty$, so $\varphi_n$ increases to $\infty$ with every step at most $\frac\pi3$.

**Conclusion.** Each of the three target sets is a union of open arcs of length $\frac{2\pi}3$ repeating with period $2\pi$. An increasing sequence tending to $\infty$ with steps $\le\frac\pi3<\frac{2\pi}3$ cannot jump over an open interval of length $\frac{2\pi}{3}$, so it lands in each of these infinitely many intervals. Hence for each player there are infinitely many, so arbitrarily large, $n$ at which that player has the highest winning probability. ∎

(Numerically, the leader changes from $A$ to $B$ at $n=3$, to $C$ at $n = 14$, back to $A$ at $n = 145$, to $B$ at $n=1608$, and so on.)

putnam-2017-a6.title: Linear algebra over the field with three elements
putnam-2017-a6.body:
Identify the three colours with the elements $0,1,2$ of $\mathbb F_3$ (any bijection). For three colours $x,y,z\in\mathbb F_3$: if all are equal or all are different, $x+y+z = 0$; if exactly two are equal, say $x = y\ne z$, then $x+y+z = 2x+z = z - x\ne0$. So a face is good exactly when the **sum of its three edge colours is nonzero**.

Let $E$ (30 edges) and $F$ (20 faces) index the vector spaces $\mathbb F_3^E$, $\mathbb F_3^F$, and let $T:\mathbb F_3^E\to\mathbb F_3^F$ send a colouring to its vector of face sums. $T$ is linear, and we must count colourings $c$ such that $T(c)$ has no zero coordinate.

**$T$ is onto.** Fix a vertex $v$; its five edges $e_1,\dots,e_5$ (in cyclic order) and five faces $F_i\ni e_i,e_{i+1}$ (indices mod 5). Put the values $2,1,2,1,2$ on $e_1,\dots,e_5$ and $0$ on all other edges. Faces not containing $v$ contain none of the $e_i$, so their sums are $0$; $F_1,\dots,F_4$ have sums $2+1$ or $1+2$, i.e. $0$; and $F_5$ has sum $e_5+e_1 = 2+2 = 1$. So the image of this vector is the basis vector of the face $F_5$. Every face arises this way (pick one of its vertices and number the edges so the face is $F_5$), so the image of $T$ contains a basis: $T$ is surjective.

**Counting.** $\dim\ker T = 30-20 = 10$, so every vector in $\mathbb F_3^F$ has exactly $3^{10}$ preimages. There are $2^{20}$ target vectors with all coordinates nonzero. Hence the number of colourings is
$$2^{20}\cdot3^{10} = 61\,917\,364\,224 .$$

**Answer:** $2^{20}\cdot3^{10} = 61917364224$

putnam-2017-b1.title: Homothety
putnam-2017-b1.body:
Distinct lines intersect iff they are not parallel.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Suppose $L_1$ and $L_2$ meet, and let $\lambda\ne0$ and $P\notin L_1\cup L_2$. The homothety $H$ with centre $P$ and ratio $\lambda$, $H(X) = P+\lambda\overrightarrow{PX}$, maps $L_1$ to a line $H(L_1)$ parallel to (or equal to) $L_1$, hence not parallel to $L_2$. So $H(L_1)$ meets $L_2$ in a point $A_2$. Let $A_1\in L_1$ be the point with $H(A_1) = A_2$. Then $\overrightarrow{PA_2} = \lambda\overrightarrow{PA_1}$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose $L_1\parallel L_2$ (they are distinct, so disjoint). Take $\lambda = 1$ and any $P$ on neither line. Then $\overrightarrow{PA_2} = \overrightarrow{PA_1}$ means $A_1 = A_2$, a point on both lines, which is impossible. So the condition fails. ∎

putnam-2017-b1.title: Linear equations
putnam-2017-b1.body:
Put the origin at $P$. Write $L_i = \{\mathbf x:\mathbf v_i\cdot\mathbf x = c_i\}$ with nonzero normals $\mathbf v_i$; $c_i\ne0$ because $P = \mathbf 0\notin L_i$. We need $\mathbf x = A_1$ with $\mathbf v_1\cdot\mathbf x = c_1$ and $\mathbf v_2\cdot(\lambda\mathbf x) = c_2$, i.e. the linear system
$$\mathbf v_1\cdot\mathbf x = c_1,\qquad \mathbf v_2\cdot\mathbf x = c_2/\lambda .$$
If the lines intersect, $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2$ are linearly independent, so the system has a solution for every right-hand side, for every $P$ and $\lambda$.

If the lines are parallel, $\mathbf v_2 = \mu\mathbf v_1$ for some $\mu\ne0$, and the system is solvable only if $\mu c_1 = c_2/\lambda$, i.e. $\lambda = \frac{c_2}{\mu c_1}$. Any other nonzero $\lambda$ gives no solution. ∎

putnam-2017-b2.title: Representations correspond to odd divisors
putnam-2017-b2.body:
**Representations.** $N = ka + \frac{k(k-1)}2$, so $2N = k(2a+k-1)$. With $\ell = 2a+k-1$, a representation with $k>1$ and $a\ge1$ gives a factorization $2N = k\ell$ with $1<k<\ell$ and $k,\ell$ of opposite parity ($\ell-k = 2a-1$ is odd and positive). Conversely, any such factorization gives the representation with $a = \frac{\ell-k+1}2$.

Write $2N = 2^eO$ with $O$ odd and $e\ge1$. A factorization into factors of opposite parity is $\{u,\ 2^eO/u\}$ with $u$ an odd divisor of $O$; the smaller factor exceeds $1$ unless $u = 1$ (note $2^eO/u\ge2$). So **$N$ has exactly $d(O)-1$ representations**, where $d(O)$ is the number of divisors of $O$.

**Applying this.** $2017$ is prime (it is not divisible by any prime up to $43$, and $45^2>2017$). With $k = 2017$, $2N = 2017(2a+2016)$, so $O = 2017\cdot O'$ where $O'$ is the odd part of $2a+2016$. Having exactly one representation means $d(O) = 2$, i.e. $O$ is prime, i.e. $O' = 1$: $2a+2016$ must be a power of $2$. (Then the unique representation is the one with $k=2017$, as $2017<2a+2016$.)

The smallest power of $2$ that is at least $2a + 2016 \ge 2018$ is $2048$, giving $a = 16$ (and $N = 2017\cdot1024$).

**Answer:** $16$

putnam-2017-b3.title: Eventually periodic digits
putnam-2017-b3.body:
Suppose $f(\frac12) = \sum c_i2^{-i}$ is rational, say with denominator $q$.

**Lemma: the sequence $(c_i)$ is eventually periodic.** Let $t_n = \sum_{i\ge n}c_i2^{n-i}\in[0,2]$. Then $t_n = 2^n\big(f(\frac12) - \sum_{i<n}c_i2^{-i}\big)\in\frac1q\mathbb Z$, so $t_n$ takes finitely many values. Also $t_n = c_n + \frac12t_{n+1}$, which forces $c_n = 0$ if $t_n<1$ and $c_n=1$ if $t_n>1$; in those cases $t_{n+1} = 2t_n - 2c_n$ is determined by $t_n$. If some $t_n\in\{0,1,2\}$, then the digits from that point on are constant (all $0$, or all $1$, or a $1$ followed by $0$s, or a $0$ followed by $1$s), so the sequence is eventually periodic. Otherwise $t_{n+1}$ is a function of $t_n$ for all $n$; since there are finitely many values, $t_n = t_{n+m}$ for some $n$ and $m\ge1$, and then $t_{i} = t_{i+m}$ and $c_i = c_{i+m}$ for all $i\ge n$.

**Consequence.** With $c_{i+m} = c_i$ for $i\ge n$ (where $n,m\ge1$),
$$f(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}c_ix^i + \frac{x^n}{1-x^m}\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}c_{n+i}x^i\qquad(|x|<1).$$
At $x = \frac23$:
- $\sum_{i<n}c_i(\frac23)^i = \frac{(\text{integer})}{3^{n-1}}$;
- $\frac{(2/3)^n}{1-(2/3)^m} = \frac{2^n3^m}{3^n(3^m-2^m)}$ and $\sum_{i<m}c_{n+i}(\frac23)^i = \frac{(\text{integer})}{3^{m-1}}$.

All denominators ($3^{n-1}$, $3^n$, $3^m-2^m$, $3^{m-1}$) are odd, so $f(\frac23) = \frac uv$ with $v$ odd. But $f(\frac23) = \frac32$ would give $3v = 2u$ with $3v$ odd, a contradiction. Hence $f(\frac12)$ is irrational. ∎

putnam-2017-b4.title: Rewrite with telescoping differences
putnam-2017-b4.body:
Let $L(x) = \frac{\ln x}{x}$ and $a_k = L(k) - L(k+1)$ for $k\ge1$.

**The series $\sum a_k$.** Its partial sums telescope: $\sum_{k=1}^na_k = L(1) - L(n+1) = -\frac{\ln(n+1)}{n+1}\to0$. Since $L$ is decreasing on $[e,\infty)$, $a_k>0$ for $k\ge3$; so $\sum a_k$ has only finitely many negative terms and converges **absolutely** to $0$. Hence it may be split and rearranged freely.

**Rewrite the summand.** One checks
$$3L(4k+2) - L(4k+3) - L(4k+4) - L(4k+5) = 3a_{4k+2} + 2a_{4k+3} + a_{4k+4} = (a_{4k+2}+a_{4k+4}) + 2(a_{4k+2}+a_{4k+3}).$$
Moreover
$$2(a_{4k+2}+a_{4k+3}) = 2L(4k+2)-2L(4k+4) = \frac{\ln2+\ln(2k+1)}{2k+1} - \frac{\ln2+\ln(2k+2)}{2k+2} = a_{2k+1} + \ln2\left(\frac1{2k+1}-\frac1{2k+2}\right).$$

**Sum.** All the series below converge, so
$$S = \sum_{k\ge0}(a_{4k+2}+a_{4k+4}) + \sum_{k\ge0}a_{2k+1} + \ln2\sum_{k\ge0}\left(\frac1{2k+1}-\frac1{2k+2}\right) = \sum_{j\ge1}a_{2j} + \sum_{k\ge0}a_{2k+1} + (\ln2)^2,$$
using $1-\frac12+\frac13-\cdots = \ln 2$. The first two sums together are $\sum_{k\ge1}a_k = 0$ (absolute convergence). Therefore $S = (\ln2)^2$.

**Answer:** $(\ln 2)^2$

putnam-2017-b5.title: Analyse the three pairs of sides
putnam-2017-b5.body:
Let $T = ABC$ with $BC = a$, $CA = b$, $AB = c$, $a>b>c$, and $p = a+b+c$. A line dividing $T$ meets its boundary in two points on two different sides (possibly at a vertex), so it cuts off a triangle at one vertex.

**Cut at vertex $B$** (points $X\in AB$, $Y\in BC$, $BX = x\le c$, $BY = y\le a$). Equal areas: $\frac12xy\sin B = \frac14ac\sin B$, i.e. $xy = \frac{ac}2$. Equal perimeters: $x+y+XY = (c-x)+(a-y)+b+XY$, i.e. $x+y = \frac p2$. From $y\le a$ we need $x\in[\frac c2,c]$, and we must solve $F(x) = x+\frac{ac}{2x} = \frac p2$ there. $F$ is convex, $F(\frac c2) - \frac p2 = \frac{a-b}2>0$, $F(c)-\frac p2 = \frac{c-b}2<0$. A convex function that is positive at the left end and negative at the right end has exactly one zero in between (two zeros would force a nonnegative value at the right end). So there is **exactly one** equalizer of this type, meeting the sides at interior points.

**Cut at vertex $A$** ($AX = x\le c$ on $AB$, $AY = y\le b$ on $AC$): $xy = \frac{bc}2$, $x\in[\frac c2,c]$, $G(x) = x+\frac{bc}{2x} = \frac p2$. Now $G(\frac c2)-\frac p2 = \frac{b-a}2<0$ and $G(c)-\frac p2 = \frac{c-a}2<0$; a convex function is at most the larger endpoint value, so **no** solutions.

**Cut at vertex $C$** ($CX = x\le a$ on $CB$, $CY = y\le b$ on $CA$): $xy = \frac{ab}2$, $x\in[\frac a2,a]$, $H(x) = x+\frac{ab}{2x} = \frac p2$. Here $H(\frac a2)-\frac p2 = \frac{b-c}2>0$ and $H(a)-\frac p2 = \frac{a-c}2>0$. $H$ has its minimum $\sqrt{2ab}$ at $x_0 = \sqrt{ab/2}$, which lies strictly inside $(\frac a2,a)$ because $\frac a2<b<2a$ (note $a<b+c<2b$). So the number of solutions is $0$, $1$ or $2$ according as $\sqrt{2ab}>\frac p2$, $=\frac p2$, $<\frac p2$.

Lines through a vertex appear only as endpoint cases, which are never solutions, so the equalizers found are distinct. Hence $T$ has exactly two equalizers iff
$$8ab = (a+b+c)^2 .$$

**Searching.** We need $2ab$ a perfect square and $\frac a2<b<a$. Checking $a\le9$: the products $2ab$ for $(a,b) = (3,2),(4,3),(5,3),(5,4),(6,4),(6,5),(7,4),(7,5),(7,6),(8,5),(8,6),(8,7),(9,5),(9,6),(9,7)$ are $12,24,30,40,48,60,56,70,84,80,96,112,90,108,126$ — none a square — while $(9,8)$ gives $144 = 12^2$. Then $(a+b+c)^2 = 576$, so $c = 24-17 = 7$, and $9<8+7$ is a genuine triangle with $9>8>7$.

**Answer:** $(a,b,c) = (9,8,7)$

putnam-2017-b6.title: Translation invariance and a recursion
putnam-2017-b6.body:
Let $p = 2017$, which is prime, and view $\{1,\dots,2017\}$ as $\mathbb F_p$. The coefficients $1,1,2,\dots,63$ sum to $1+\frac{63\cdot64}2 = 2017 = p$.

**Fix $x_0 = 0$.** Adding the same $t\in\mathbb F_p$ to every coordinate keeps the entries distinct and changes the linear form by $t\cdot p\equiv0$; each orbit of this translation action has exactly $p$ tuples and contains exactly one with $x_0 = 0$. So the answer is $p\cdot f$, where $f$ is the number of tuples of **distinct nonzero** $x_1,\dots,x_{63}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{63}ix_i = 0$.

**Lemma.** Let $a_1,\dots,a_k$ be positive integers with $a_1+\dots+a_k<p$. The number $f(k)$ of $k$-tuples of distinct nonzero elements of $\mathbb F_p$ with $\sum a_ix_i = 0$ depends only on $k$, and
$$f(1) = 0,\qquad f(k) = \frac{(p-1)!}{(p-k)!} - k\,f(k-1)\quad(k\ge2).$$
*Proof.* $f(1)=0$ since $a_1x_1 = 0$ forces $x_1 = 0$. For $k\ge2$, consider the $\frac{p!}{(p-k)!}$ tuples of distinct elements. Translation by $t$ changes the form by $t\sum a_i$ with $\sum a_i\not\equiv0$, so each orbit (of size $p$) contains exactly one solution: there are $\frac{(p-1)!}{(p-k)!}$ solutions with distinct entries. In such a solution at most one entry is $0$; those with $x_i = 0$ correspond to solutions in the other $k-1$ variables (coefficient sum still $<p$) with distinct nonzero entries, $f(k-1)$ of them for each $i$. Subtracting gives the recursion. $\square$

**Solving the recursion.** Put $G(k) = \frac{p\,f(k)}{k!}$. Since $\frac{p}{k!}\cdot\frac{(p-1)!}{(p-k)!} = \binom pk$, we get $G(1) = 0$ and $G(k) = \binom pk - G(k-1)$. By induction (with Pascal's rule $\binom pk = \binom{p-1}k + \binom{p-1}{k-1}$),
$$G(k) = \binom{p-1}{k} + (-1)^k(p-1).$$

**Answer.** The coefficients $1,\dots,63$ sum to $2016<p$, so the count is
$$p\,f(63) = 63!\,G(63) = 63!\left(\binom{2016}{63} - 2016\right) = \frac{2016!}{1953!} - 63!\cdot2016 .$$
(Sanity check of the method: for $p = 7$ and $4$-tuples with coefficients $1,1,2,3$, the formula gives $3!\big(\binom63 - 6\big) = 84$, which agrees with a direct count.)

**Answer:** $\dfrac{2016!}{1953!} - 63!\cdot 2016$
